blocks.text: X-rays is a type of electromagnetic radiation of much shorter wavelength, about 10⁻¹⁰m. In order to observe the effects of diffraction, the grating spacing must be of the order of the wavelength of the radiation used. The regular array of atoms in a crystal forms a natural diffraction grating with spacing that is typically≈10⁻¹⁰ m. The scattering of X-rays from the atoms in a crystalline lattice gives rise to diffraction effects very similar to those observed with visible light incident on ordinary grating.

The study of atomic structure of crystals by X-rays was initiated in 1914 by W.H. Bragg and W.L Bragg with remarkable achievements. They found that a monochromatic beam of X-rays was reflected from a crystal plane as if it acted like mirror. To understand this effect, a series of atomic planes of constant interplanar spacing d parallel to a crystal face are shown by lines PP′, P₁P′₁, P₂P′₂, and so on, in Fig. 9.18.

blocks.text: Suppose an X-rays beam is incident at an angle θ on one of the planes. The beam can be reflected from both the upper and the lower planes of atoms. X-rays diffraction has been very useful in determining the structure of biologically important molecules such as hemoglobin, which is an important constituent of blood, and double helix structure of DNA.
